title: Sessions are server-issued opaque handles, never signed client-readable claims
description: A successful token consumption issues a session by writing a server-side record and returning an opaque handle to the client. The handle is base64url of at least 24 bytes of cryptographically random entropy; it carries no identity claim, no scope claim, no signed payload, and no data the client can decode. Identity, scope, and expiry are looked up server-side from the record on every request. No JWT-shaped token, no self-describing bearer, and no client-decodable envelope is issued on any authenticated code path. The session-lifetime contract is: a sliding idle window bounded by `sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds` (default 3600, refreshed by every validated request without changing the handle value), a fixed absolute lifetime bounded by `sessionAbsoluteLifetimeSeconds` (default 604800, never refreshed once issued), and server-side revocation as the only truthful invalidation (client-side cookie clearing alone never invalidates). A validated request whose stored `issuedAt + sessionAbsoluteLifetimeSeconds` is in the past is refused as unauthenticated even if the sliding window has not elapsed. Defaults are declared on ADR-504 and overridable per project.
rationale: A signed client-readable token turns every session into a JWT-shaped design problem: key rotation, revocation lists, clock skew, algorithm-confusion attacks. An opaque handle plus a server-side record makes revocation a delete, makes scope changes atomic, and keeps the secret material where the operator can actually see it.
